title: Request and Response Objects
description: Dive into HttpRequest and HttpResponse – what you can do with them.

slides.title: The HttpRequest Object 📨
slides.content:
When Django receives a request, it creates an `HttpRequest` object that contains metadata about the request. It is passed as the first argument to your view.

Common attributes:
- `request.method` – HTTP method (GET, POST, etc.)
- `request.GET` – Query string parameters (dictionary‑like)
- `request.POST` – Form data
- `request.user` – The current user (if authenticated)
- `request.session` – Session dictionary

slides.title: Accessing Request Data

quizData.question: How do you access query string parameters (e.g., `?name=John`) in a Django view?
quizData.explanation: `request.GET` is a dictionary‑like object containing all GET parameters.

slides.title: The HttpResponse Object 📤
slides.content:
Your view must return an `HttpResponse` (or subclass). You can set content, status code, and headers.

Common subclasses:
- `HttpResponse` – generic response
- `JsonResponse` – returns JSON data
- `HttpResponseRedirect` – redirects to another URL
- `HttpResponseNotFound` – 404 (but usually you'd use `raise Http404`)

slides.title: Creating Responses
Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use `shortcuts` for common tasks

Instead of manually creating HttpResponse objects, use `render()` for templates, `redirect()` for redirects, and `get_object_or_404()` for database lookups.
